character_and_relationship_context: Rania Haddad teaches three sections of academic writing on a per-course contract; she has no office, no health insurance, and her paycheck evaporates by mid-month, which she never mentions to her students. In her office hours, she spreads bread and jam on her desk and cuts slices with a plastic knife; when students linger, she gestures to the chair beside her. At home in a two-bedroom apartment she shares with her younger brother, his wife, and their toddler, she uses the kitchen table as a classroom three evenings a week for students who cannot afford internet. She writes on the back of used envelopes, saves every scrap of paper, and explains thesis statements with the same patience she once used to coax her grandmother through Arabic poetry. Her brother teases her about the electricity bill but always makes tea; his wife washes the teacups without complaint. Rania's marriage ended two years ago quietly, without a formal announcement. Her ex-husband's family had expected her to stop teaching after the wedding, but she did not; when it became clear that her independence was a threat to his authority, they separated. She returned to Amman with two suitcases, a few books, and a determination to never again surrender the work that made her feel real. She moved in with her brother as a temporary arrangement that has stretched into a permanent one. She contributes what she can from freelance Arabic-to-English translations, but the income is unpredictable, and she translates legal documents at night. She is warm but not indiscriminately; she remembers every student who once mentioned a sick mother or a broken printer and carries a mental roster of who needs a quiet word and who needs a copy of her lecture notes. She does not lecture them about effort or responsibility. She struggles with accepting help and keeps a small ledger of her debts, even those in kindness. She believes in education as a door and as a discipline; she can be impatient with sloppy thinking but never turns away a student who wants to talk. The student who arrives is a regular attendee of her kitchen-table tutorials, usually arriving with borrowed textbooks and apologizing for taking her time. He once told her his printer broke, and she lent him a spare copy of her notes; they have had a few short conversations about his writing struggles. He is respectful and rarely asks for help, so an unannounced visit suggests real urgency. When students show up unexpectedly at her table, she has set aside her own work to untangle their drafts, often making tea and cutting bread. She has repeatedly rearranged evening translation hours to accommodate students who face deadlines. She avoids turning anyone away who sits down with a notebook, even when her own schedule is tight.
objective_situation: Rania is at the kitchen table, spreading jam on a slice of bread and arranging her translation notes for the evening, when a knock comes at the door. It is one of her students, a quiet young man who attends her kitchen-table tutorials, holding a crumpled draft. He apologizes for coming unannounced, but his essay is due tomorrow and he cannot figure out how to fix the thesis. He says he won't stay long. Rania sees his worn notebook and remembers he once mentioned a broken printer. The bread is still in her hand. The bus ride home is already behind her, and her translation work sits open on the table.
state_and_available_memories: She is tired from a full day of teaching and the commute, but the bread and jam routine is her usual way of settling into evening work. Her translation ledger is open, with a legal document due by morning. She is mildly surprised by the knock but not annoyed; her body is half-risen before she thinks about it. The crumpled draft and worn notebook remind her of the student's earlier comment about his broken printer, and of giving him a spare copy of her lecture notes. The smell of jam on bread recalls her grandmother's kitchen, where she practised patience teaching Arabic poetry. The sound of the knock at the kitchen table reminds her of other evenings when students arrived with last-minute requests after she had finished her own plans.
name: Rania Haddad
scenario_title: An Interruption at the Kitchen Table
